name: Surgical orthodontics

lead: Surgical orthodontics combines braces with corrective jaw surgery to fix bite problems, airway issues and facial imbalance, including receding chins, underbites, overbites and asymmetry. Appearance is among the stated goals, and the jaw position and profile change visibly.

Orthodontists align the teeth, and an oral and maxillofacial surgeon cuts and repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw or chin, usually through the mouth, fixing it with plates and screws. Studies report high post-surgical satisfaction, alongside depressive reactions during recovery in some patients.

paras: Treatment is coordinated between an orthodontist and a surgeon, and some patients have surgery before braces. Initial healing takes 2 to 6 weeks and bone union a further 2 to 4 months. The term is also used for surgically facilitated orthodontics, such as corticotomy, which aims to speed tooth movement.
Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness from nerve injury, which usually recovers within about three months. It is major surgery with weeks to months of recovery.

chain: Jaw bone is cut and repositioned
angle.text: Looksmaxxers consider jaw surgery with braces to correct bite, airway and facial imbalance, including recessed or overlong jaws. The jaw bone is repositioned, so the change in jaw position and profile is visible afterward.

lead: Surgical orthodontics usually means orthodontic treatment combined with orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery, in which an oral and maxillofacial surgeon cuts, moves and realigns the upper jaw, lower jaw or chin, typically through the mouth, in coordination with an orthodontist who aligns the teeth [1]. The term is also used for surgically facilitated orthodontics, such as corticotomy, which aims to speed tooth movement [2][3].

For appearance, the appeal is that it changes the skeleton beneath the face. Moving a recessed lower jaw or chin forward, setting back a protruding jaw, shortening or lengthening the midface, correcting a tilted bite plane or evening out an asymmetry alters the profile, the lower-face proportions, the lip relationship and the bite at the same time [1][4][5][6]. Reviews describe both functional and aesthetic goals [7], and in looksmaxxing communities jaw surgery sits in the category known as hardmaxxing, the most structural and invasive end of the spectrum [8].

Medical indications include skeletal jaw discrepancies, underbites, overbites, open bites, receding chins, sleep apnea, temporomandibular joint problems and facial asymmetry [1]. Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness from nerve injury, which is usually temporary [1]. Psychological studies from the 1980s reported high satisfaction after surgery alongside depressive reactions in some patients during recovery [9][10], and a systematic review of body dysmorphic disorder estimated a weighted prevalence of 11.2 percent among orthognathic surgery patients [11].

paras: Orthognathic surgery corrects jaw and lower-face problems involving growth, bite, airway and symmetry. Surgeons usually work from inside the mouth, so scars are not visible on the face, and they cut the jaw bone, move it to a planned position and fix it with titanium plates and screws [1]. The surgery is normally one stage of a longer orthodontic treatment rather than a stand-alone procedure [1][5].

Two terms are often used interchangeably in patient discussions: orthognathic surgery, which names the surgery, and surgical orthodontics, which names the combined plan. A separate usage covers surgically facilitated orthodontics, where a minor bone procedure around the teeth, such as corticotomy or piezoelectric decortication, is added to shorten orthodontic treatment time rather than to move the jaws [2][12][13].

Wikipedia reports that one of the first published jaw-surgery cases was by Simon Hullihen in 1849, that jaw osteotomies date to the 1940s, and that Hugo Obwegeser popularised the sagittal split of the lower jaw [1]. Obwegeser (1920-2017), who trained in Vienna and Graz and worked with Harold Gillies in 1951-52, is credited in Wikipedia with developing the modern Le Fort I osteotomy and, in 1969 or 1970, describing the simultaneous two-jaw operation; he presented his techniques to North American surgeons in 1966 [14].

The Le Fort name comes from the French surgeon René Le Fort, who described patterns of midface fracture in the early 1900s by dropping cadavers from different heights; the horizontal Le Fort I fracture pattern gave its name to the upper-jaw osteotomy [15][5]. A 1985 development noted by Wikipedia was the use of osteotomies for more severe deformities such as receding chins and joint pain, and local anaesthesia with intravenous sedation, introduced by Raffaini in 2002, reduced hospital stays [1]. A 2023 review lists advances of the past twenty years: computer-assisted planning, patient-specific fixation, wider use for upper-airway obstruction and changes in how orthodontics and surgery are sequenced [7].
Surgeons choose the operation by the region being corrected.

Bilateral sagittal split osteotomy corrects mandibular retrusion and prognathism by splitting the lower jaw behind the teeth and sliding the tooth-bearing segment forward or back, then fixing it with plates and screws [1]. Older methods wired the jaw shut for four to five weeks; Wikipedia says prolonged wiring is generally no longer required [1].

The Le Fort I osteotomy separates the maxilla horizontally above the tooth roots so it can be moved forward, up, down or tilted. A 2021 review describes its indications, contraindications, preoperative assessment, technique and complications, and stresses that facial analysis and close collaboration with the orthodontist are central [5]. It is used for conditions such as vertical maxillary excess, sometimes called long face syndrome [1].

Genioplasty moves the chin bone forward, back, up or down, and is often done with jaw surgery or on its own [1][16]. A 2023 review notes that chin position strongly influences lower-face aesthetics and so is assessed on its own merits in orthognathic planning, with attention to stability, fixation and complications [4].

Bimaxillary surgery moves both jaws in one operation. Maxillomandibular advancement, which moves both jaws forward and is often paired with a tongue-advancing procedure, is used for obstructive sleep apnea, and Wikipedia describes it as one of the most effective surgical treatments for that condition [17]. A 2021 review of asymmetry describes three-dimensional diagnosis and virtual planning as increasingly useful for symmetry cases [6].

Rapid palatal expansion uses a screw-activated appliance, adjusted weekly for up to eight weeks, to widen a narrow upper jaw [1]. Newer techniques named in Wikipedia include surgery-first sequencing, clear aligners in place of braces, and custom implants [1]. Community discussions of palate expansion before jaw surgery use the abbreviation MARPE [18].

Treatment traditionally starts with up to a year of braces to align the teeth before surgery; a surgery-first approach, in which the operation comes before most tooth movement, has been described in case reports, including one for mandibular prognathism [1][19]. Planning uses radiographs, photographs and 3D prediction software [1].

A systematic review of virtual planning screened 392 articles and included twelve; it found average translation differences of under 2 mm for both jaws between plan and outcome, with the most common protocol being cone-beam CT combined with intra-oral scans of dental casts [20]. A review of virtual setups in orthodontics covers planning and evaluation in the same digital workflow [21]. A 2023 randomised trial compared clear aligners with fixed appliances after jaw surgery, measuring gum health and quality of life [22].

Wikipedia gives initial healing as two to six weeks, with bone union and remodelling taking a further two to four months; swelling mostly resolves within weeks but some lasts months, and full recovery after complex cases can take up to a year [1]. Patients typically follow a liquid or soft diet and often lose weight, take pain medication for about a week, and return to work around two to six weeks [1]. Any jaw immobilisation lasts about one to four weeks [1].

Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, nausea, infection (up to 7 percent in one cited summary, lowered by perioperative antibiotics) and facial numbness from injury to the nerves, usually recovering within about three months and rarely permanent [1]. Some movements, such as maxillary impaction, carry higher risk [1]. Genioplasty complications include swelling, temporary lip numbness and, less often, infection or nerve damage [16][4].

Psychological effects have been studied since the early 1980s. Researchers followed 55 patients from a month before to nine months after surgery and found satisfaction, self-esteem and body image high, but depressive reactions at the fixation-removal stage [9][10]. Separately, a systematic review of body dysmorphic disorder estimated a prevalence of 11.2 percent in orthognathic surgery settings compared with 1.9 percent among adults in the community, and described the condition as poorly identified [11]. Wikipedia notes that psychological assessment is occasionally required before surgery [1].

A 9-month longitudinal study of 55 patients found satisfaction, self-esteem and body image high after surgery [9]. A follow-up study compared 90 surgical patients with 66 who considered surgery but chose conventional orthodontics, measuring mood states [10]. A 1986 study examined personality characteristics as predictors and consequences of surgical and conventional orthodontics [23]. A review of orthodontic treatment and quality of life reports that patients seek treatment largely for appearance and social acceptance [24].

Methodology studies include the virtual-planning systematic review [20], a randomised trial of aligners versus fixed appliances after surgery [22] and a comparison of three facebow and articulator systems for surgical planning [25]. Registered trials on surgically facilitated orthodontics include corticotomy effects on tooth movement (completed, 10 participants) [2], piezoelectric decortication in adults (completed, 20) [12], acceleration of lower crowding (completed, 38) [26], a pain and acceptance study of periodontally accelerated osteogenic orthodontics (completed, 16) [13] and a grafting-material trial (not yet recruiting, 24) [3]. A randomised trial of surgically facilitated orthodontic treatment was withdrawn [27], and a registered study of speech before and after orthognathic treatment is recruiting 180 patients [28]. A CBCT evaluation looked at alveolar bone changes after corticotomy-assisted orthodontics [29].

Wikipedia places jaw surgery under hardmaxxing and says maxillofacial surgery is frequently proposed and discussed among looksmaxxers; it also cites a 2025 article in Body & Society on maxillofacial surgery in looksmaxxing and a 2024 Guardian feature on the movement [8]. Mewing, the tongue-posture practice, is described by Wikipedia as a social-media alternative to orthognathic surgery according to the title of a 2019 Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery commentary, and the same page reports that most orthodontists do not regard it as a substitute [30].

On looksmax.org, threads discuss single-jaw versus bimaxillary plans, the age at which surgery is feasible, palate expansion, choice of surgeon and insurance. One poster with a recessed jaw asked whether to have one jaw or both moved, and replies advised consulting an orthodontist and noted that bimaxillary surgery is usually done at age 18 or later [18]. Another member posted a long surgical history, including a bimaxillary operation for sleep apnea that he said had a good functional but poor aesthetic result, and described bone protrusions at the cuts being shaved to a flush jawline [31]. A thread titled on the risks of jaw surgery lists permanent numbness, chronic lip pain and altered sensation among complications its author collected from patient stories, and links to a community post on the risks of surgery generally [32].
A 2017 study of YouTube videos on orthognathic surgery examined the quality of content patients encounter online [33].

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums jaw surgery is the reference point for what skeletal change is achievable, and threads mix plans and consultations with warnings about complications [18][31][32].

claims.claim: Jaw surgery is the most direct way to change facial structure
Mewing or jaw posture can replace surgery
Jaw surgery brings lasting numbness and other complications that are underreported
The aesthetic result can differ from the functional one
Jaw surgery improves self-esteem and mood
Jutting the jaw forward in advance helps insurance cover surgery
Patients with body dysmorphic concerns are over-represented in surgery
